accuracy.evidence: Wording checked against CCSS 7.SP.A.1 (generalisations from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative; random sampling tends to produce representative samples) and the DfE GCSE Mathematics subject content (infer properties of populations or distributions from a sample, knowing the limitations of sampling). Lab numbers are exact: 48+36+24+12 = 120 of 240 = 50%; all of Year 7 is 48/60 = 80%.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the known errors at 12-14: bigger is always better (all 60 of Year 7 still says 80%; 400 from Year 11 in m6), trusting voluntary response polls with many votes (website poll, online lunch poll at 90%), mixing up population and sample (sort step, p1), expecting a random sample to hit the exact truth (five samples vary 45-60%), and random meaning haphazard.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagsample is the only lab with a 240-dot school population whose answers stay hidden until sampled: a draggable 20-student box reveals one corner, random draws light scattered dots, and every sample drops a marker on a 0-100% estimate strip against the census value. lab_distinct gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners build the idea from evidence: the handy box gives 75%, 40% and 10% depending on where it lands, random samples of 20 then cluster round the dashed 50% census line, size 80 samples cluster tighter, and the 60-student Year 7 diamond sits at 80% to show size does not cure bias before the method-judging step applies it.

predictions.evidence: Three committed predictions: what asking all 240 is called (census), whether Sam's Year 7 form at 80% overstates the whole school (lower), and whether five random samples of 20 will agree exactly (no, they differ but stay close to 50%); each is then shown on the estimate strip.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions (gym survey, which is the population, website poll, best sample of 800, why not a census, two random samples 45% and 55%) with shuffled options; wrong answers give tagged hints for size, swap, bigger and not-representative slips rather than a bare wrong.

readability.evidence: Learner kid text meets the 6.5 grade target and adult text meets 9.5 per validate_lessons. Precise terms are each introduced in plain words: population is everyone you want to know about, census asks all of it, random means the same chance for each person.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a term or a worked case (240 Hilltop students, 50% census, website poll, gym survey); no stock openers; the content gate's filler phrase and overlap checks pass against all existing lessons.

mobile.evidence: Walkthrough passed on iPhone 13 and desktop with all 5 tasks completed via Show me; 360 px screenshots in light and dark show the 24 by 10 grid, year labels, legend and estimate strip without overlap, the sort columns wrap card text to column width, and every action also has a full-width button.

accessibility.evidence: axe clean in light and dark on both viewports. Yes and no use shape (filled dot vs ring) as well as colour; estimate markers use square, circle and diamond for handy, random and biased; every drag or tap has a button twin, and each sample result is spoken through the live region.

sources: Moore, D. S., McCabe, G. P. and Craig, B. A. Introduction to the Practice of Statistics (voluntary response and convenience samples, sampling variability)
